title: Minnesota Bans Crypto ATMs After Residents Report Nearly $1 Million in Scam Losses
excerpt: The state becomes the third in the US to prohibit cryptocurrency kiosks as the FBI reports $333 million in nationwide ATM-linked fraud losses last year.
body:
• Minnesota's ban on cryptocurrency ATMs took effect August 1, making it the third US state — after Indiana and Tennessee — to prohibit the machines
  • Residents reported 134 complaints and nearly $1 million in losses from crypto kiosk scams between 2023 and 2025
  • Existing machines must be removed by December 31; the state had roughly 350 licensed kiosks
  • The FBI reported $333 million in nationwide losses tied to crypto ATMs last year, with seniors disproportionately targeted

The Ban Takes Effect

Minnesota on Saturday became the third US state to ban cryptocurrency ATMs after Governor Tim Walz signed legislation in May prohibiting the machines that state officials called a "fast-growing form of scam" disproportionately targeting seniors. The law, which took effect August 1, bars the installation of new crypto kiosks immediately and requires all existing machines — roughly 350 across the state — to be removed by December 31.

The kiosks, commonly found in gas stations and convenience stores, allowed users to convert cash into cryptocurrency almost instantly. Operators included companies such as Bitcoin Depot and Coinflip.

The Damage in Numbers

Between 2023 and 2025, the Minnesota Department of Commerce recorded 134 complaints tied to cryptocurrency kiosk scams, totaling nearly $1 million in reported losses. In 2025 alone, there were 70 cases with more than $540,000 lost — an average of nearly $6,800 per transaction. Officials emphasized that many incidents go unreported because victims are embarrassed at having been deceived.

"When victims call our office after a crypto kiosk scam, you can hear the panic and shame in their voices. By the time victims realize they were deceived, the emotional and financial damage can be devastating."

— Paul Haas, Investigator, Minnesota Department of Commerce

Scammers typically impersonate law enforcement officers or government officials, using emotional manipulation — including fake "grandparent emergencies" and romance schemes — to pressure victims into converting cash at nearby kiosks. Once a transaction is recorded on the blockchain, it cannot be reversed, and the funds are extremely difficult to trace.

When Regulation Was Not Enough

Minnesota had tried a regulatory approach first. In 2024, it became the first US state to enact laws governing crypto kiosks, requiring fraud warning signs, a $2,000 daily transaction limit for new customers, and a 14-day refund window for scam victims. Commerce Department officials testified that scammers routinely bypassed these protections by coaching victims to use existing accounts or directing them to machines in neighboring Wisconsin.

House File 3642, sponsored by Representative Erin Koegel, passed both legislative chambers with broad bipartisan support. Representative Harry Niska, who had co-authored the 2024 regulatory framework, told the House floor that the machines are "used for really one of two purposes: crime through money laundering or crime through being the backend of some sort of a scam."

A Growing National Problem

Minnesota joins Indiana and Tennessee in banning cryptocurrency kiosks entirely. The FBI reported $333 million in nationwide losses tied to crypto ATMs last year, and the American Association of Retired Persons reported in February that 17 states had laws requiring operators to implement consumer protections.

Cryptocurrency transactions lack the consumer protections that govern traditional banking — there is no central institution that can freeze, dispute, or reverse payments, and no federal chargeback process comparable to credit card disputes. Congress is currently working on legislation to bring digital currency under more stringent federal regulation.

Commerce Commissioner Grace Arnold framed the ban as a public safety measure. "Criminals take advantage of that instinct, using urgency and fear to scam people in vulnerable moments," she said. "Cryptocurrency kiosks allow that money to disappear almost instantly."

For immigrant communities, including Indian Americans who may rely on cash-based financial services, the Minnesota ban is a reminder that convenience in digital finance can come at a cost — and that the regulatory landscape around cryptocurrency remains in rapid flux.
nri_angle: Indian Americans and other immigrant communities who use cash-based financial services should be aware of growing cryptocurrency kiosk fraud risks as regulation remains in flux.
